Stages

Each stage lists what to learn, which CSES sections to finish, which filters to practise from, what to aim for in contests, and an exit checklist. Move on only when the checklist is done. CSES counts come from the CSES tab.

Interview track: Google Software Engineer III (L4)

The plan runs interview coding on Tue–Thu evenings (LeetCode Top Interview 150, timed, in a plain doc), design at 12:30 on weekdays (3 HLD, 2 LLD a week), and behavioral prep or a mock on Saturday afternoons. Coding finishes around Feb 4, design around Feb 13, mocks from Nov 7. Apply when every box below is ticked, not on a date.

How practice changes by stage

All CSES problems

Checks here and in the daily plan are the same. A date next to a problem means it is scheduled that day. Up to 1600, stick to the first four sections.

Codeforces practice filters

Each link opens the problemset with the tag and rating range set, sorted by most solved. Green rows on Codeforces are ones you already solved. The counter fills from your evening checkboxes.

Other practice

USACO Guide dashboard: sign in there and mark modules as you read them. Silver is stage 1, Gold is stage 2, Platinum is stage 3. Most readings in this plan point at its modules or at CP-Algorithms.

The daily AtCoder problem is picked from ABC C–F by difficulty and is already in the plan. For more: AtCoder Problems table (colour by difficulty, set your handle to hide solved ones) and the difficulty list. Live ABC: Saturdays 17:30 IST as a rule, some weeks Sunday. Schedule.

Rules

  1. Before coding, rewrite the statement in one plain line, then work sample 1 by hand. If you can't do both after 15 minutes, read the Note section and the samples again. Understanding the statement is half the problem right now.
  2. Reading day: the reading takes the whole 09:00 block. Write a 5-line summary and the template code in your own words before touching problems.
  3. Page problems come easiest first. Problems more than 300 above the topic's band are parked and come back later as a "page revisit". Nothing is dropped.
  4. Spaced review comes first in the morning: re-solve one earlier problem from a blank file, then one new problem on the same idea. +1 day, +7 days and +30 days after each reading.
  5. Not sure a greedy holds? Don't guess. Write the brute force (try every order or subset for n up to 8) and run stress/stress.sh. If it survives 300 random tests, submit.
  6. Interview coding: a plain doc, no IDE, no autocomplete. Talk out loud. State the approach and complexity before you write code. Dry-run on the example, then submit. Already solved it before? Do it again timed anyway.
  7. Time-box each problem to 45 minutes. Then read the editorial, close it, and code it yourself.
  8. Ask for help in steps, not for the answer. From Claude or the editorial, take one hint at a time: first "which topic is this?", then "what is the key observation?", and only then the solution. Stop reading as soon as you can continue alone.
  9. Tap "needed help" on any problem where you used a hint, the editorial or Claude. It comes back the next day as a re-solve from a blank file. That re-solve is where the learning happens.
  10. Before you type: write the idea as 2–3 comment lines. Estimate the number of states or operations. If it's above about 10⁸, shrink the search first (for example, one queen per row, not one per square).
  11. Before you submit, run four checks. Bounds: multiply n by the max value, and use long long above 2·10⁹. Impossible cases: when is the answer NO or −1? Code vs idea: walk sample 1 through the code by hand and compare it with your comment lines. Edges: try n = 1, all values equal, and the max values.
  12. Second WA on the same problem? Stop guessing. Write the brute force and run stress/stress.sh from your CP folder. Fix the failing case it prints, then resubmit.
  13. Rounds start at 20:05, right after your meeting. Do every one live. If the meeting runs over, register anyway and start late. Skip the round only if work is on fire, then do it virtual in the next 10:45 block.
  14. CSES stuck past 45 minutes: skip it. You're missing a technique. Come back after the next topic.
  15. Write one line per missed idea in the day's log box.
  16. LeetCode daily is a 30-minute cap. It keeps interview patterns warm; it does not move your rating. If a Hard runs past 30 minutes, read the editorial and move on.
  17. Missed a day? Don't catch up. Do today's plan and move on. If the day was a holiday or you were ill, open it and press "Mark as off day": that day's study plan moves to the next day of the same kind (weekday or weekend) and everything after it shifts by one, the day drops out of the totals, and the streak skips it. Undo pulls the plan back. Be honest with it; it's for days you couldn't, not days you didn't.
  18. LeetCode contests come in at stage 1: Weekly on Sunday 08:00 IST, Biweekly on Saturday 20:00 IST. Do Weekly when there is no Codeforces round the night before; skip Biweekly if it clashes with a round.
